noi_dung:
Demons Come to Help You Cultivate the Way

I once said: "If one can sit still for a brief moment, it surpasses building seven-jeweled stupas as many as the Ganges' sands." Someone sitting in the Chan Hall idly thinks: "Sitting still for a moment holds more merit than building seven-jeweled stupas"; then thinking back and forth, he cannot sit still for even an instant, and so gains not a shred of merit! Why? It is like mistaking the finger for the moon—seeing only the finger pointing at the moon without seeing the moon—and then claiming limitless merit! Limitless? You are just sitting there with limitless discursive thoughts!

Then he says: "I can radiate light shining throughout the universe! I can radiate light shining throughout the universe!" That state needs no thinking from you, no announcing from you—it needs your practice. Only if you can truly become pure and enter samadhi can you radiate light shining throughout the universe. Unable to enter samadhi, idle fancies do no good at all. Thinking back and forth is all discursive thought, eighty-four thousand miles from reality.

Someone else thinks: "How can I enter samadhi? How can I become enlightened?" If you harbor such discursive thoughts, then by no means can you enter samadhi or become enlightened. Why? Because you are applying effort only skin-deep, not applying effort in prajna wisdom. You are altogether seeking outward. Never seeking inward, you will never find it.

Be electrotherapists to help this world. Rescue the beings living in this polluted air so they can become Buddhas in fresh, clean air. Now you must sit in stillness, without so many discursive thoughts, and I hope you clearly understand this. I have already explained to you the electrotherapy that makes the air pure. Try it and see how it works?

Today is the second day of the Chan Session—have you "set out on the road" yet? "Setting out" means taking the road of Right Enlightenment, the road of Bodhi. Have you raised up the phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name" yet? Have you let go of discursive thoughts yet? If you have not yet raised up "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" then hurry and do it. Train like "a cat stalking a mouse," patiently watching for the mouse. Be like "a mother hen hatching her eggs," wholeheartedly mindful of the chicks about to hatch. Be like "a dragon guarding its pearl," carefully and single-mindedly holding the precious pearl tight. Only by applying effort at all times can accomplishment be hoped for.

We practice "eating one meal a day, sleeping without lying down"—an ascetic practice I dare say is the finest in the world. Especially during a Chan Session: sitting twelve hours a day, circling six hours. Such bitter practice requires meditators to eat their fill. Thus in China, whenever a Chan Session was held, every night each person was given two big steamed buns, and everyone loved it. But here we have no such custom. So at lunch, eat a little extra—eat your fill, to have strength for circling or running.

Buddhist precepts stipulate "eating once at midday"—that is, eating only one meal a day, at noon (twelve o'clock). Later this changed to "not eating past noon"—after twelve noon no meals are taken, though morning porridge for breakfast is allowed. Since it is not eaten after noon, this is no violation of the precepts.

During a Chan Session, if you do not eat enough you will lack the strength to sit in Chan, to circle, or to run, and so may retreat. Why? If you investigate Chan into the night, your stomach will growl and scold you for being so selfish—knowing only how to cultivate, caring only about enlightenment, ignoring it and making it suffer. It asks what kind of Way you cultivate, without even a shred of compassion. Then it refuses to cooperate with you, and you easily retreat in resolve, no longer wanting to cultivate, wasting all your former effort. Hence during a Chan Session you must eat your fill to have the energy to seek liberating wisdom.

Today I will tell you the story of "Eating Buns During a Session." This is a true story, not made up. At Tiantong Monastery in Ningbo, China, there was an abbot named Miyun. He was a Good Knowing Advisor with the Clear Eye. The Venerable Weina was also a Good Knowing Advisor with the Clear Eye. But the Venerable Weina's compassion was vast, while the Abbot's compassion was narrow. Abbot Miyun's style was "a Mahasattva who minds nobody's business," while the Venerable Weina stood for "a Bodhisattva who loves minding people's business." Since the two held different views, their conduct clashed.

During the Session, everyone sat vigorously in Chan, seeking liberating wisdom. One night, this compassionate Venerable Weina saw that the assembly, too hungry, had no spirit left for sitting. Some were sunk in stupor, some with scattered minds, and if not dozing then "slumped sitting." Normally a sitting person measures about three feet tall, but with stomachs too empty to sit straight, they hunched over, barely a foot tall—hence "slumped sitting." Once this set in, no one could keep sitting. Seeing this, the Venerable Weina took pity and, wishing to preserve the assembly's strength, entered samadhi and used his spiritual powers to slip into the kitchen and steal some scorched rice, distributing a little to each person. When the sitting ended, everyone opened their eyes to find a piece of scorched rice on their laps, and quietly ate it all up. For "people are iron, rice is steel"—once eaten, everyone regained their spirits. While circling, no one felt tired. No longer like before, when empty stomachs made circling impossible and they had to sit aside to rest.

After the compassionate Venerable Weina stole scorched rice two days running to feed the assembly breakfast, on the third day the Abbot discovered the theft and expelled him from the monastery.

It happened thus: on the morning of the third day, the monk in charge of the kitchen found that yesterday's scorched rice had vanished, and suspected the rats had eaten it. Since it was his duty, he reported it to the Abbot for instructions. The Abbot said: "Very well, catch that rat!" That night the Abbot entered samadhi to contemplate, and discovered that the Venerable Weina had stolen the kitchen's scorched rice while in samadhi. He then hid the Venerable Weina's physical body beneath a sitting bench. When the Venerable Weina left samadhi, his "house" (his body) was nowhere to be found. Searching everywhere, at last he found his body lying beneath a bench, and pulled it out. The Abbot then said: "What are you doing? You are quite the big rat. You dare steal scorched rice from the kitchen? Do you know you have violated the precepts? Whoever violates the precepts must be expelled! Tomorrow you must go. We can keep you here no longer!"

The Venerable Weina said: "Venerable Sir, expel me if you must, but I beg one thing of you, and hope you will grant it."

The Abbot asked: "You are about to leave—what more do you ask?"

The Venerable Weina said: "Meditators must eat their fill before they can apply effort in cultivation. If they do not eat enough, they surely cannot cultivate. That is why I slipped into the kitchen to steal scorched rice for the assembly—not for myself. I hope the Abbot will be compassionate and give each person two buns every evening. If so, I will bow to you in gratitude. Once I am gone, I will have no more regrets!"

The Abbot thought it over and saw the sense in it: "Very well! I will grant your request." From then on, whenever a Chan Session was held, each person received two buns in the evening.

The Venerable Weina then asked the Abbot: "Venerable Sir, where should I go?"

The Abbot replied: "Go to Sichuan province and build a Way-place. The Dharma protectors there have affinities with you."

Then the Venerable Weina used his spiritual power of unimpeded travel to reach Sichuan. Seeing two tall cassia trees with lush branches and leaves, he sat in Chan between them. Many Dharma protectors and laypeople saw him sitting beneath the trees, recognized him as a true cultivator, a virtuous high monk, and so built a monastery beneath the two cassia trees, naming it "Two Cassia Hall." There he transmitted the Dharma and accepted disciples. Later, a great many Chan investigators became enlightened, and he became the founding Patriarch.

Investigating Chan is like drinking water—hot or cold, only you know. When your skill is steady, you know it yourself; when your skill is not yet mature, only you know that too. Whoever's skill is steady and mature must keep striving without pause. Whoever has gotten nowhere must not be lazy. During the Session you must let go of everything. There is a saying:

"Take it up, and let it go."

"Take up" what? Take up the phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"

"Let go" of what? Let go of all discursive thoughts. Only by letting go of discursive thoughts and scattered thinking will wisdom arise. Unable to let go of discursive thoughts, your effort will bear no fruit.

During these seven days you must be valiant and vigorous, without a trace of laziness or a shred of doubt. Apply effort together. When your effort reaches "seeing neither self nor others," you will become enlightened. When your effort reaches "neither form nor emptiness," you will merge with the Tathagata. If you have not yet understood the state of "neither form nor emptiness," you should truly be ashamed.

Why does effort fail to correspond? Because habits and tendencies from limitless kalpas past are far too deep; thus the mind wishes to head for the Bodhi road while the body refuses to advance, always wanting to retreat. Know that the heavier your habits, the deeper your karmic obstacles, the more you must let go of discursive thoughts. Letting go of discursive thoughts is not hard—you need only forget yourself, and discursive thoughts vanish at once. Only because the "I" remains can you not forget yourself.

Cultivating in the Chan Hall, you must cultivate so that "above, you do not know there is sky; in between, you do not know there are people; below, you do not know there is earth." Sky, earth, and people gone, east, west, south, and north dissolved—then not a single thought arises, and the whole true mind appears. You will attain "the great function of the whole."

Giving rise to discursive thoughts all day, your skill will never correspond. So you must apply effort to where not a single thought arises. Walking, not knowing you are walking; standing, not knowing you are standing; lying down, not knowing you are lying down; sitting, not knowing you are sitting. Of walking, standing, lying, and sitting, knowing nothing at all:

Eating rice all day, yet not swallowing a single grain.

Wearing clothes all day, yet not putting on a single thread.

Then you merge into one with empty space. Merging into one with empty space, you suddenly interpenetrate; abruptly you will understand all things. That is the state of sudden enlightenment.

Sudden enlightenment comes from ordinary effort—applying effort to the point of correspondence, then suddenly becoming enlightened. Without ordinary effort there can be no sudden enlightenment. Like a child after birth: hearing speech day after day, one day it naturally learns to speak. When it utters its first words, it is much like our moment of enlightenment. When it starts to walk, that first step too may be compared to our enlightenment. How does it take that first step? Because day after day it watches adults walking back and forth, and the scene perfumes its mind, until it naturally toddles forth. Our effort must be the same—apply effort today, apply effort tomorrow. Continuing thus, when the skill ripens, with no more ideas arising and discursive thoughts wholly ceased, you will become enlightened.

Enlightenment through day-by-day effort, hour-by-hour effort, until the skill ripens and enlightenment suddenly comes—that is enlightenment through this life's cultivation.

Someone asks: "I see that fellow applies no effort at all, yet shortly after coming to the Chan Hall he suddenly becomes enlightened. Why is that?" That case is rather special. It is because, though in this life he applies no effort, in a past life he already cultivated. And not ordinary cultivation—hour after hour, minute after minute he cultivated, falling short of enlightenment by just a little. Thus in this life, meeting the right conditions, he at once becomes enlightened.

Though sudden enlightenment is instant enlightenment, it requires good roots nurtured in past lives. Like farming—sow in spring, till in summer, and only in autumn reap the harvest. If in spring no seed is sown, how could autumn hold a harvest? There is a saying:

"As you till, so shall you reap."

We who cultivate the Way must be the same—whether enlightened or not, valiant and vigorous, striving forward. Hoping that in a final moment we will gain the result and recognize our "original face."

Why can we not recognize our "original face"? Because the mark of self (the "I") is not yet removed, and selfishness not yet ended. If the mark of self were gone and selfishness ended, you could recognize your "original face" at once.

If you do not wish to recognize your "original face," that is no problem—cultivate or not, it makes no difference, for you have no hope at all. But one who cultivates the Way must surely have hope. The hope of clearly knowing where you came from and where you are going—of knowing where you were born from and where you go after death. If you wish to know what your "original face" is like, you must not fear suffering, hardship, or difficulty—only then can you return to the origin and attain the "indestructible vajra body."

What do we do in the Chan Hall? We forge the "indestructible vajra body." Once it is the "indestructible vajra body," this body surely knows no more suffering, no more pain. So if we keep fearing suffering and pain, we can never accomplish the "indestructible vajra body." This indestructible body is forged through training. And the work we are doing here is precisely forging the "indestructible vajra body"—training this body to be firm, never to decay.

Hearing this, someone thinks: "I cultivate not for this 'stinking skin bag.' What use is forging it into indestructibility?" Not wrong! Your reasoning is quite right; but the "indestructible vajra body" I speak of is not this "stinking skin bag." What is it then? It is the "indestructible vajra body" of the own-nature—also the Dharma body and the wisdom life—precisely the "indestructible vajra body" of the originally pure own-nature.

Remember: cultivating the Way is no easy matter. As soon as you wish to cultivate the Way, demons come to disturb you. These demons come not from one place alone, but from all directions. Some are sickness demons, some are affliction demons; there are heavenly demons, human demons, ghost demons, and monster demons besides. The demons come from where you least expect or know, shaking your resolve for the Way and making you retreat in practice. They use every means to lure, intimidate, and threaten you, forcing you to retreat, lose your samadhi power, and quit cultivating altogether.

When your sitting reaches a fair level, demons will come to test your Way-power. Sometimes they transform into handsome men or beautiful women to seduce you—if your mind is unmoved, you pass the test; if your mind moves, you will fall. This is of utmost importance—remember it well! One false step, and the regret lasts a thousand lifetimes!

When states appear to test the cultivator, we must examine whether the state is true or false. By what method? Very simple: recite "A Di Đà Phật", single-minded and undisturbed, without discursive thoughts. If the state is false, it will slowly fade away. If the state is true, the more you recite, the more clearly it appears. Whoever sits in Chan without knowing this method will go astray and fall under demonic influence, and their Way-karma will dissolve. Others, supposing they have entered demonic states, will miss their chance at enlightenment.

When young I heard it said: "To cultivate the Way is to meet demons." I did not believe it, and arrogantly declared: "No demon frightens me! I fear no monsters or ghosts at all!" I thought saying so was harmless, nothing to fear. Who knew that before long demons truly came to disturb me. What demon? The sickness demon! That time I fell gravely ill, unconscious for seven or eight days, knowing nothing at all. Only then did I know my skill was insufficient and I could not pass the test. Monsters and ghosts, heavenly demons and outside ways—none frighten me; only the sickness demon—I could neither subdue it nor endure it. Therefore, one who cultivates the Way must not boast or preen, claiming to fear nothing. If you are smug and self-satisfied, trouble comes at once!

How should one who cultivates the Way be? Humble and cautious, as if walking on the edge of a deep abyss or treading on thin ice. At all times utterly careful, highly alert—only then can you cultivate the Way. In short, "speak little, sit much"; that is the root of cultivation.

Whose aid enables the cultivator to accomplish the Way-karma? The demons'! Just as a blade must be whetted to be sharp, the cultivator shines forth the light of wisdom thanks to demons' help. So regard demons as Dharma protectors. Hence the saying:

Meeting matters, awake to matters: transcend the world. Meeting matters, confused by matters: fall and sink. (Seeing matters, understanding them: transcend the world; Seeing matters, deluded by them: suffer a fall.)

If you can awaken, meeting each state with penetrating understanding, you will transcend the world. If you cannot awaken, deluded by whatever you meet, you are bound for the hells. So one who cultivates the Way does not fear meeting demons—only fears lacking samadhi power. Demons come to help you, to test you, to see whether you have skill and samadhi power. If you have skill and samadhi power, then no matter what demon it is, none can shake your spirit.

In cultivation, always hang the words "the question of birth and death" before your brows, always thinking of how to end birth and death. Know that nothing is more important than "the great matter of birth and death." If birth and death are unresolved, you will not know why you were born or where you go after death. So until you have truly penetrated "the question of birth and death," you must apply effort vigorously; otherwise you will forever be bound by the wheel of birth and death, never to be liberated.

On the path of the Way, hold this "question of birth and death" in mind, and regard the demons as Dharma protectors helping your cultivation. Whoever scolds you or beats you is helping you cultivate. Whoever gossips about you or makes things hard for you is also helping you cultivate. In short, when adversity comes, simply go along with it and endure. Regard them all as friends come to aid you, and afflictions will end. Once afflictions end, wisdom arises. With true wisdom, no demon can shake your mind.

Why are we shaken by demonic states? Because our wisdom is not yet perfected. With wisdom imperfected, whatever we meet deludes us and we fail to see clearly—the marks of self, others, living beings, and a life all arise, and afflictions rise along with them. With true wisdom, such problems would never occur!
tieu_de: Demons Come to Help You Cultivate the Way
